findings.title: Count and fetch can observe different database snapshots
findings.description: The admission count and the subsequent row fetch are separate statements under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level. Concurrent inserts can therefore make the fetch return more rows than the count admitted, so the configured ceiling does not reliably bound the response size. The same count-then-fetch pattern is used for trades at lines 160–163. The reader module’s claim that a concurrent insert can make the response only one row over the ceiling is not guaranteed: a batch may add multiple rows between those statements.

findings.title: Large response construction and encoding run on the event loop
findings.description: After the database work leaves the executor, building up to 75,000 Pydantic records and serializing the response with JSON or msgpack happen synchronously inside the async handler. This is CPU-bound work well beyond the sub-millisecond limit in the Python rules and can block other requests on the event loop; the ceiling-sized candle response is measured at about 35 MB. The load tests exercise ceiling-sized requests, but do not test how this response-processing work affects concurrent requests.

findings.title: Trades watermark is described as the newest stored trade
findings.description: The OpenAPI description says `tape_complete_through` is the created time of the newest stored trade, but `tape_facts` populates it from the sync-state watermark. The schema migration documents that watermark as the end of the last fully walked window, explicitly not the newest stored trade. For a quiet market, those instants can differ, so clients may misinterpret the coverage fact.
